extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of moral/social history and classical studies
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarises the evaluative principles, legal maxims, and moral criteria used in a historical treatment of Roman social, legal, and domestic life (gladiatorial shows, slavery, family authority, Stoic influence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacles of death are brutalising and demoralising
rubrics_metrics.description: Under every form and modification the gladiatorial spectacles and similar shows were 'brutalising, savage, and detestable' and the sight of blood and suffering is necessarily and essentially depraving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support: Seneca denounced the games with passionate eloquence; Plutarch condemned combats of wild beasts on the ground of sympathy for sentient beings. Anti-patterns/defences noted: proponents argued these spectacles were ancient religious rites or useful discipline when the combatants were guilty. The text contrasts these defences with moralist condemnations and notes that few pagan writers fully reached the position that such spectacles were inconsistent with humanity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-combat continence and stoic endurance as moral dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: The severe continence required of gladiators before combat, contrasting with general Roman licentiousness, invested them with a kind of moral dignity; Fathers even selected the gladiator as the closest approximation to a Christian model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: narratives of gladiators calmly facing death, fathers and Church Fathers observing the moral effect. Use: this feature was taken to exemplify courage, self-mastery, and a model of moral fortitude despite the overall atrocity of the spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: If combatants are guilty, public fighting can be justified as discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument (noted by Cicero): when guilty men are compelled to fight, the spectacle presents a discipline against suffering and death and may be defensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a common apologetic justification rather than an accepted moral conclusion; Seneca and others refute it. Use: represents one evaluative criterion proponents used to defend violent spectacles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural law principle: all men are equal by nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoic-derived legal/philosophical maxim (Ulpian): 'as far as natural law is concerned all men are equal.' Paul: 'Nature has established among us a certain relationship.' Florentinus: slavery is contrary to the law of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides jurisprudence and moral judgment: provides the philosophical foundation for extending rights and humane treatment, and for later legal reforms. Quasi-formal citation: this was quoted by Roman jurists and used as the ideal underpinning legal change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial presumption in favour of freedom where slavery is doubtful
rubrics_metrics.description: Maxim among Roman lawyers: in every doubtful case where the alternative of slavery or freedom was at issue, the decision of the judge should be towards the latter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a concrete legal rule deriving from Stoic natural-law principles; used to protect individuals from being treated as slaves where status ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law should embody abstract principles and equity, not only empirical rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Roman legislation was modelled on philosophical abstractions—laying down principles of right (law of nature) and rules of equity to guide judges when the law was silent or ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides legislative and judicial reform: encourages formulation of general principles rather than only ad hoc enactments. Examples: Theodosius/Justinian compilations; Stoic influence provided ideal standards for judges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parents should win children's confidence before commanding obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: Educational error: parents who seek to command obedience before winning confidence create unhappy homes; absolute paternal authority chills affection and arouses resentment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: Roman paterfamilias' power (right to take life, dispose of property) is criticized as defeating its own object. Reform guidance: diminishing paternal despotism and promoting reciprocity of duty improves domestic virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive paternal power undermines filial affection and social welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: The Roman law granting fathers absolute authority (even over life and property of children) produced resentment and harmed filial affection; legal limits and protections for children improve family relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical reforms cited: prohibition of infanticide, withdrawal of the right to kill adult children (Alexander Severus), protection of children's property in some cases, annulment of wills that disinherited legitimate sons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cruelty to animals is often an index of human cruelty but is not infallible
rubrics_metrics.description: Cruelty to animals naturally indicates and promotes habits that lead to cruelty to men, but there are notable exceptions (e.g., Spinoza's amusement with flies; some cultures kind to animals yet cruel to humans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological caution: use animal-cruelty indicators as suggestive but not conclusive evidence of a person's or people's humanity; consider cultural anomalies and counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social practices and mass enslavement foster increased barbarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Large-scale slavery, luxury, gladiatorial spectacles, and servile wars contributed to a deterioration in the condition of slaves and a savage indifference to suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Causal claim for moral analysis: the increase in numbers of slaves and luxury removed mitigating social bonds and aggravated cruelty. Use in evaluation: assess institutions and cultural practices for their systemic effects on moral behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal safeguards for slaves are required to prevent wanton cruelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific legal protections developed: Petronian law forbade condemning a slave to wild beasts without judge's sentence; laws forbade exposing sick slaves (with recovery granting freedom); masters who wantonly killed slaves could be punished as murderers; statutes provided a judge for slave complaints; mutilation for sensual purposes forbidden; emperor's statue served as asylum for slaves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These concrete legal measures are presented as moral/legal standards for humane treatment. They exemplify how statute and judicial oversight can constrain masters' abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowing peculium and enfranchisement mitigates slavery's harshness
rubrics_metrics.description: Customs such as recognising a slave's peculium (private property) and extensive enfranchisement (a well-conducted captive might expect freedom in ~six years) alleviated some harms of slavery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy implication: legal and customary avenues to property and freedom lessen degradation; used in the text to temper wholesale condemnations of ancient slavery and to explain variability in slave conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion and social sanction can check extreme abuses
rubrics_metrics.description: Public reprobation isolated and punished extreme acts of cruelty by masters; conspicuous cases were pointed at and insulted in the streets, and the populace sometimes rebelled against harsh official sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative tool: moral pressure from society and reputation served as an informal mechanism to curb abuses where law was insufficient. Example: Seneca’s claim that masters who ill-treated slaves were publicly shamed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophical engagement in public life sustains civic virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoic maxim that the sage should take part in public life promoted patriotism and produced virtuous rulers who exerted influence for the cause of virtue (e.g., the 'five good emperors').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative claim: moral/philosophical teaching should aim to shape public institutions and cultivate leaders; anti-pattern: sectarian withdrawal from public affairs leads to diminished civic influence (contrasted with Neoplatonists/Catholics who became mystics/hermits).
